subject: <Your-Repo>
$comment: TEMPLATE: copy to <repo>/proofs/modules.json, set `subject`, and replace the `modules` array with one entry per model your check.ps1 checks. What the proof leg COSTS, declared per module, so that a growth in prover time is named rather than discovered when CI times out. `proofs/check.ps1` (through `proofs/kit/check-proof-leg.ps1`) reads this file: every green CHECK line prints the module's measured seconds beside its budget, and a run over budget prints a named COST warning — never a failure on its own, because prover time varies by machine and by load and a budget is a smoke detector rather than a gate. `check.ps1 -Strict` promotes the warnings to a red leg for a session that wants one. This is NOT `proofs.json`: that file is the claims ladder — what is proved, tested and assumed, at a closed set of levels — and a wall-clock budget is a claim at none of those levels and is not per-claim but per-module. Coverage is checked BOTH ways: a module the leg checks with no entry here, and an entry here for a module the leg does not check, are each a COST warning naming what to do. Hand-authored; the seeding rule below says how a number is arrived at, and bumping one is a recorded act. Each entry also carries a `floorSeconds`, and that number is a GATE rather than a smoke detector: a module that verifies in less than its floor fails the leg on the spot, because a run faster than the module can possibly be is not evidence of speed but of a cache that was not cold. The two rules sit in `seeding` and `floorSeeding` below, and the asymmetry between warning above and failing below is argued in the second of them.

seeding.rule: budgetSeconds = max(2 x the slowest observed cold-cache run, minimumBudgetSeconds), rounded up to the next 10s.
seeding.$comment: The tolerance is applied ONCE, here, when a number is seeded — `check.ps1` multiplies nothing, so the pair it prints is the measurement against the ceiling and there is no second arithmetic to hold in your head. Seed from the SLOWEST observed cold run rather than the median: concurrent sessions on one machine can inflate a cold check by ~1.8x with nothing about the tree changed, so a budget seeded from the median fires on a busy afternoon and teaches a reader to ignore it. `minimumBudgetSeconds` is the floor UNDER THE CEILING, for the sub-5s modules where 2x is inside ordinary process-start noise; it is a different thing from an entry's `floorSeconds`, which is the per-module time floor below, and the two are named apart deliberately.
seeding.$namingNote: This key was `floorSeconds` until Phase 155, which is the same word the per-entry time floor uses for the opposite thing — one is the smallest a BUDGET may be, the other the smallest a RUN may be. Renamed rather than documented: a skeleton that ships a collision ships it to everyone who copies it.

floorSeeding.rule: floorSeconds = the FASTEST genuine cold run ever observed, halved, rounded DOWN to the whole second; 0 for a module whose fastest genuine cold run is under 5s.
floorSeeding.$comment: The floor is the budget's mirror and the two are deliberately NOT symmetric in what they do. A budget is a ceiling and a smoke detector: an overshoot is a true measurement of a true cost, so it warns and the leg stays green. A floor is a gate: `check.ps1` FAILS the leg on the spot, naming the module and the time, because a module that verified faster than it can possibly verify has not told you it is fast — it has told you the measurement is worthless, and everything measured after it shares the apparatus. Implausibly fast is the one direction in which a lie looks like good news. Seed from the FASTEST observed rather than the median, and halve on top, for the mirror of the budget's reason: a floor that fires on a fast quiet machine teaches a reader to ignore it, and the failure this catches lands at or near ZERO seconds, so an enormous margin costs nothing in detection. The `zeroBelowSeconds` rule is for the modules where halving lands inside process-start noise: a positive floor there would be a coin toss, and an explicit 0 is a different statement from an absent one and reads as one. An ABSENT `floorSeconds` is a cost finding rather than a failure — a sibling adding a model should no more go red for a floor nobody has measured than for a budget nobody has measured. `check.ps1 -NoFloor` is the deliberate opt-out for a machine genuinely that fast, and it says so in the log. Re-seeding a floor DOWNWARDS is the same recorded act as bumping a budget upwards: the new number, the `fastestSeconds` it came from, and your phase.

contentionSeeding.rule: threshold = a number above the median ratio of a measured QUIET pass on the SLOWEST machine that runs this leg, and at or below the median ratio of the contention worth naming. Place it high: a false label suppresses a real regression, where a missed label costs only what the leg did before.
contentionSeeding.quietFactor: <the median factor YOUR quiet pass measured — re-seed `threshold` from it>
contentionSeeding.$comment: TEMPLATE: the numbers here are the reference repository's, not a measurement of your leg — re-seed `threshold` and `quietFactor` from your own machines before trusting a label. At the end of every run the leg reports the MEDIAN, over the modules the working tree did NOT change, of that module's measured seconds divided by the `measuredSeconds` its entry records — the run's CONTENTION FACTOR. Above this threshold every cost finding from that run is LABELLED a contended pass where the closing verdict prints it, and a labelled finding is explicitly NOT a re-seed obligation: re-seeding a budget from a contended run raises a ceiling to fit a slow afternoon, which is how a budget stops meaning anything. `-Strict` promotes only the UNLABELLED findings. Nothing is multiplied into a measurement — the seconds a green line prints stay the wall clock, and the factor sits beside them. THE SCALE IS NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE. `measuredSeconds` is not a typical cost: by `seeding`'s own rule it is the SLOWEST cold run ever observed for that module, so the ratio's neutral point sits well BELOW one — the reference repository's quiet pass measures x0.29, not x1, and its recorded contention incidents sit near x1.0 because their `measuredSeconds` were seeded under exactly that load. A threshold chosen as though 1.0 meant `normal` would sit above any contention your leg can experience and would never fire. Measure one quiet pass and one contended pass of YOUR leg, put the number between them, and record both figures here. `minimumSamples` is the smallest set the median may be taken over; below it the leg reports the factor as not computed rather than taking a median of one. A module whose `measuredSeconds` is under `floorSeeding.zeroBelowSeconds` does not vote, because at whole-second resolution a one-second module's ratio is quantisation rather than signal. AN ABSENT BLOCK IS NOT A FINDING: the factor is still computed and printed, nothing is labelled, and the line names this block to seed — so an adopter that has measured nothing yet gets one extra number and no new warning.

modules.note: One entry per model. `measuredSeconds` is the observation the budget was seeded from and `fastestSeconds` the one the floor was seeded from — keep both, because a bump is only readable against the number it replaced. An OPTIONAL `contentionFactor` may sit beside `measuredSeconds`: the contention factor the leg reported on the pass that measurement came from, so a later reader can tell a budget seeded quiet from one seeded busy. It is provenance only, never computed with, and an absent one reads as `not recorded` rather than as 1 — which is why this worked entry does not carry one. The note says what the module is, what makes it expensive or cheap, and anything a future reader must check BEFORE reading a bump as ordinary growth (a scoped `--z3rlimit`, an `--ext context_pruning` that could have been lost, an SMT-pattern cliff).
